guidingQuestion: How does energy set matter moving within and between Earth's four major systems?
hook: Every few minutes a geyser in Iceland hurls scalding water high into the sky, and the energy behind each blast comes from hot rock deep beneath the ground.

sections.title: Key Science Concept: The Flow of Energy and Matter Through Earth's Systems

objectives.text: Identify Earth's four major systems and the three main layers of the geosphere, and sort real parts of Earth into the system, or systems, they belong to.
sections: Key Science Concept: The Flow of Energy and Matter Through Earth's Systems

objectives.text: Explain how heating and cooling change a material's density and how, together with gravity, that drives convection cells in mantle rock, ocean water and air, and tell convection apart from conduction and radiation.
Trace where each system gets its energy, from the sun or from Earth's hot interior, and follow energy and matter as they cross from one system into another.
sections: Key Science Concept: The Flow of Energy and Matter Through Earth's Systems

objectives.text: Use physical and conceptual models of Earth's systems, name what a model leaves out, and evaluate how Biosphere 2's data exposed a problem that scientists then traced and used to improve the design.

keyIdeas: Scientists model Earth as four overlapping systems: the geosphere (all the rock and metal from the surface to the center), the hydrosphere (all the water, including ice, groundwater and vapor), the atmosphere (the blanket of gases) and the biosphere (every living thing plus the places where life can survive).

The geosphere has three main layers. The crust is thin, cool and rigid. The mantle is thick, hot rock that is solid yet creeps very slowly. The core is mostly iron and nickel. Each layer is denser than the one above it.

Warming usually makes a material spread out and become less dense, and cooling makes it denser. Gravity tugs harder on the denser material, so it sinks and shoves the less dense material upward. Warm at the bottom plus cool at the top keeps a convection cell turning.

Energy moves in three ways in this lesson: conduction between materials that touch, convection when a fluid or slowly flowing solid carries energy as it circulates, and radiation, which carries energy as light, even across empty space.
Two power sources run Earth's systems. Heat from the planet's hot interior drives convection in the mantle, while the sun supplies most of the energy that moves ocean water, air and living things.

Sunlight lands more directly near the equator than near the poles, so air and ocean water warm in the tropics and cool near the poles. That uneven heating keeps giant air and ocean convection loops moving around the globe.

Matter and energy cross system borders constantly: water evaporates into the air and falls back as rain, plants take carbon dioxide from the air, and eruptions throw rock into the sky. In the biosphere, matter cycles, but energy flows through and leaves as heat.

Biosphere 2 was a sealed physical model of Earth's systems built in Arizona. Its data revealed falling oxygen, which scientists traced to soil bacteria, showing how testing a model exposes problems that the next design can fix.

glossary.definition: The system made of all of Earth's solid and molten rock and metal, from the outer surface down to the very center.
The system made of all of Earth's water in every form: salty oceans, lakes, rivers, ice, groundwater, cloud droplets and invisible water vapor.
The envelope of gases held around Earth by gravity, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, which thins out gradually with height instead of ending at a sharp edge.
The system made of every living thing on Earth together with all the places in the rock, water and air where living things can survive.
The geosphere's thin, cool, stiff outer shell; it is the least dense of the three main layers.
The thick, hot layer of rock between the crust and the core. It is solid, yet hot enough to creep very slowly over long spans of time.
Earth's hot, very dense center, made mostly of the metals iron and nickel; it is the densest of the three main layers.
How much mass is packed into a given volume of a material, such as grams per cubic centimeter. Less dense materials float on denser ones.
Energy passing directly between materials that touch, always from the warmer one to the cooler one.
Energy carried along by moving material: warmer, less dense material rises while cooler, denser material sinks, forming a loop called a convection cell.
Energy traveling as light, which can cross empty space or pass through clear materials such as air and glass.
A real, built object or setup that copies how a system works, usually at a smaller scale, so it can be tested.
A drawing, diagram or equation that represents how a system works, rather than a built copy of it.
A system that matter cannot enter or leave. Energy, such as sunlight and heat, can still cross its boundary.

explorer.title: Four Systems, One Planet
paragraphs: Picture Earth as four systems woven together. The geosphere is all the rock and metal from your sneakers down to the planet's center. The hydrosphere is all the water: salty seas, glaciers, rivers, groundwater and even invisible vapor. The atmosphere is the blanket of gas, and the biosphere is every living thing plus the places it can live.

Slice the geosphere like an apple and you find three main layers. The crust is a thin, stiff shell. Below it, the mantle is a thick zone of hot rock that is solid but creeps very slowly. At the center sits the core, made mostly of iron and nickel. Density climbs as you go down, from the light crust to the heavy core.

The systems overlap. Water vapor is water, so it belongs to the hydrosphere, and it is a gas mixed into the air, so it belongs to the atmosphere too. A fish lives in the biosphere while swimming through the hydrosphere.

Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water. Only a few percent is fresh, and most of that fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice caps. The air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and it gets thinner and thinner with height until it fades into space.

diagram.caption: Earth's four systems at a glance (sizes are the textbook's rough model values)
diagram.alt: A table with three columns: system, what it includes, and rough size in the textbook model. Geosphere: rock and metal from the surface to the center, in three layers called crust, mantle and core; about 6,370 kilometers from the surface to the center. Hydrosphere: all water, including oceans, ice, groundwater and vapor; a band about 20 kilometers thick in the textbook model. Atmosphere: the gases around Earth, mostly nitrogen and oxygen; thins out gradually, fading by about 10,000 kilometers. Biosphere: all living things and the places they live; a thin zone that overlaps the other three.
rows: Rock and metal from surface to center: crust, mantle, core
All water: oceans, ice, groundwater, vapor
Thins out, fading by about 10,000 km
Living things and the places they live
A thin zone overlapping the other three

explorer.watchOut: The four systems are not sealed boxes; a single thing, like water vapor, can belong to two systems at once. Also, the textbook calls the core a rock layer, but it is mostly metal (iron and nickel), and its outer part is liquid.

explorer.title: Convection: When Heat Sets Matter Moving
paragraphs: Density means how much mass is packed into each bit of space. When a material warms up, its particles spread out a little, so the same mass takes up more room and the density drops. When it cools, it packs back together and gets denser.

Gravity pulls harder on denser material, so cool, dense stuff sinks and squeezes warmer, less dense stuff upward. Heat a fluid from below and cool it from above, and you get a loop: warm material rises, cools, sinks, warms again. That loop is a convection cell.

Convection happens in pots of water, in the oceans, in the air and even in the mantle, where solid rock creeps so slowly that one loop takes millions of years. In every case the material itself moves, carrying its energy along.

Convection is only one way energy travels. In conduction, energy passes between materials that touch, like a hot core warming the rock resting on it. In radiation, energy travels as light, which is how sunlight crosses empty space to reach Earth.

diagram.caption: One trip around a convection cell
diagram.alt: A loop of five steps with arrows from each step to the next. Step 1: material is warmed near the heat source. Step 2: it expands and becomes less dense. Step 3: it rises. Step 4: far from the heat source it cools and becomes denser. Step 5: gravity pulls it back down, which brings it back to step 1 near the heat source.

explorer.watchOut: "Heat rises" is a shortcut that misleads. Energy spreads from warmer to cooler places in any direction; what rises is warmer, less dense material pushed up by denser material sinking around it. Convection always means material moving, so not every energy transfer is convection. One more catch: fresh water below about 4 °C gets less dense as it cools further.

explorer.title: Two Power Sources and Lots of Border Crossings
paragraphs: Almost all the energy that moves things around on Earth comes from two places. Heat from the planet's hot interior travels outward and drives convection in the mantle, feeding volcanoes and geysers. The sun delivers far more energy to the surface, and it powers most of the motion in the oceans, the air and the living world.

Because Earth is round, sunlight hits the tropics nearly straight on and strikes the poles at a slant, spread over more ground. Air and water heat up near the equator and lose heat near the poles, which keeps huge convection loops of air and ocean water circling the globe.

Matter and energy cross from system to system all day long. Sunlight warms the sea and water evaporates into the air; the vapor cools, condenses into cloud droplets and falls as rain. Plants take carbon dioxide from the air. Eruptions toss rock and ash into the sky.

In the biosphere, producers such as plants capture sunlight and store its energy in food. That energy passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then decomposers, with some leaving as heat at every step. Decomposers return matter to the soil for plants to reuse, but they cannot send energy back. Matter cycles; energy flows through.

diagram.caption: Energy sources and some border crossings between Earth's systems (arrows point from where something starts to where it goes)
diagram.alt: A web of six boxes: the Sun, Earth's hot interior, and the four systems. Arrows: the Sun to the hydrosphere, labeled warms water by radiation; the Sun to the atmosphere, labeled warms air unevenly; the Sun to the biosphere, labeled captured by producers. Earth's interior to the geosphere, labeled conduction and convection. Geosphere to atmosphere, labeled eruptions throw rock and ash into the sky. Hydrosphere to atmosphere, labeled evaporation. Atmosphere to hydrosphere, labeled rain and snow. Atmosphere to biosphere, labeled carbon dioxide taken in by plants.

explorer.watchOut: The textbook's biosphere diagram labels the arrow from decomposers back to producers "energy and matter." Only matter makes that return trip; energy leaves living things as heat, so producers need fresh sunlight. Also, a few deep-sea communities run on chemical energy instead of sunlight, so "all biosphere energy comes from the sun" is nearly, not completely, true.

explorer.title: Testing a World Under Glass
paragraphs: Scientists use two kinds of models. A conceptual model is a drawing, diagram or equation, like a cutaway of Earth's layers or the rule density = mass ÷ volume. A physical model is something you actually build and test, like a tank of water warmed at one end and chilled at the other.

Biosphere 2, built in the Arizona desert, was a giant physical model: a sealed glass building holding a small rainforest, desert, ocean, marsh, savanna and farm. Its builders wanted to learn whether people could someday live in a sealed habitat on another world.

Sealed meant closed to matter: air, water and soil stayed inside. Energy still crossed the walls, because sunlight poured in through the glass and heat escaped. Researchers measured the model for two years and used the data to keep adjusting it.

About sixteen months in, the data showed oxygen dropping and the crew felt tired. The culprit was bacteria in the very rich soil, which used oxygen as they broke down organic matter. Later research found that the carbon dioxide they released was partly soaking into the building's exposed concrete. A failed prediction like this is still useful: it shows what the next design has to fix.

diagram.caption: Two kinds of models in this lesson
diagram.alt: A table comparing two model types. Conceptual model: examples are a cutaway drawing of Earth's layers and the equation density equals mass divided by volume; it is good for explaining relationships quickly; its limit is that it cannot be run or measured like the real thing. Physical model: examples are Biosphere 2 and a water tank heated at one end; it is good for collecting real data and testing designs; its limit is that it is smaller and simpler than Earth, so some processes behave differently.
rows: Cutaway of Earth's layers; density = mass ÷ volume
Cannot be run or measured like the real thing
Biosphere 2; a water tank heated at one end
Smaller and simpler than Earth, so some processes behave differently

explorer.watchOut: A model copies only selected parts of a real system. A pot of swirling water shows the idea of mantle convection, but mantle rock is solid and takes millions of years to complete a loop. And Biosphere 2 was "closed" only to matter: sunlight and heat crossed its walls the whole time.

reviewFlags.issue: The vocabulary box and Section 1 call the core a 'rock layer' and say the core is the hottest layer because it is under intense pressure from the layers above. The core is mostly metal (iron and nickel) with a liquid outer part, and its heat comes mainly from heat left over from Earth's formation and from radioactive decay; the pressure is what keeps the inner core solid.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content describes the core as mostly iron and nickel metal and never says pressure causes its heat. The core-temperature-from-pressure claim is not used in any question. The density order of the layers (crust least dense, core densest), which the textbook gets right, is tested in L10-Q03.

evidence.locator: Section 1. The Geosphere, The Layers of the Geosphere and Figure 1A
evidence.supports: The crust is the least dense layer, the core is made mostly of iron and nickel and is the densest layer, and the core lies about 3,470 km from the bottom of the mantle to the center.

evidence.title: Core
evidence.supports: The core is almost entirely iron and nickel metal, the outer core is liquid, the inner core stays solid because of pressure, and the core's heat comes from radioactive decay and leftover heat from planetary formation.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 and Figure 2 explain the global ocean loop with temperature alone (polar water cools and sinks). Real deep-water formation depends on temperature and salinity together: sea ice forming leaves salt behind, making cold polar water saltier and denser. Winds also drive the surface currents.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content keeps the textbook's temperature-driven picture as a simplified model and adds that saltier water is also denser. L10-Q18 (multi) asks which changes make polar seawater sink and keys both cooling and becoming saltier, with the NOAA source for salinity.

evidence.locator: Section 2. The Hydrosphere, Energy and the Cycling of Matter in the Hydrosphere, Figure 2
evidence.supports: Polar air cools ocean surface water, which sinks to form deep currents that flow back toward the equator, while warm equatorial water stays near the surface.

evidence.title: Currents Tutorial: The Global Conveyor Belt
evidence.supports: Polar surface water is chilled and also gets saltier because salt is left behind when sea ice forms; the colder, saltier water is denser and sinks.

evidence.title: What is the global ocean conveyor belt?
evidence.supports: The conveyor is driven by thermohaline currents (temperature and salinity) in the deep ocean together with wind-driven surface currents.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 4 says most of the energy and matter in the biosphere is 'cycled' from organism to organism, the Lesson Summary repeats this, and Figure 4 labels the arrow from decomposers back to producers 'energy and matter.' Energy does not cycle: it flows one way and leaves organisms as heat. Decomposers return matter (nutrients) to producers, not energy.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says matter cycles while energy flows through and leaves as heat (key idea 7, Science Explorer card for L10-O3 with a watch-out naming the Figure 4 arrow). L10-Q23 asks learners to repair that exact arrow label. No question uses 'energy cycles' as a fact.

evidence.locator: Section 4. The Biosphere, Figure 4 (Energy and Matter in the Biosphere)
evidence.supports: Producers capture solar energy; herbivores, carnivores and decomposers obtain energy by eating; decomposers break down dead organisms and wastes. The figure draws a loop of arrows each labeled energy and matter.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 46.2 Energy Flow through Ecosystems
evidence.supports: Energy flows directionally through ecosystems and is lost as metabolic heat at each transfer.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 46.3 Biogeochemical Cycles
evidence.supports: Energy enters ecosystems as sunlight and leaves as heat, while the matter that makes up living organisms is conserved and recycled.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 4 and the Lesson Summary say energy in the biosphere originates with the sun, stated as an absolute. Nearly all food chains start with sunlight, but deep-sea hydrothermal-vent communities are built on chemosynthetic bacteria that use chemical energy instead.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says 'most' or 'nearly all' biosphere energy starts as sunlight. L10-Q22 is framed as 'in most food chains' and its limitations name the vent exception.

evidence.supports: Energy enters the biosphere from the sun and is captured by producers such as plants, which make their own food.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 46.2 Energy Flow through Ecosystems
evidence.supports: Chemoautotrophs, mainly bacteria in places without sunlight such as hydrothermal vents, use chemical energy (for example from hydrogen sulfide) and supply energy to the rest of those ecosystems.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 3 says the atmosphere contains small amounts of other 'elements, including argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapor.' Carbon dioxide and water vapor are compounds, not elements. The photo panel's percentages (78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon, 0.04% carbon dioxide, 0.06% trace gases including water vapor) are dry-air values: water vapor varies from near zero to about 4%, and carbon dioxide keeps rising (NOAA lists about 0.042%).
reviewFlags.resolution: Content names nitrogen and oxygen as the main gases and treats CO₂ and H₂O as compounds. L10-Q07 tests only that air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen and that weather happens in the lowest, densest air. No question tests the trace-gas percentages.

evidence.locator: Section 3. The Atmosphere, The Parts of the Atmosphere and photo panel
evidence.supports: The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, has no sharp upper boundary, grows less dense with height, and its weather happens in the lowest, densest levels.

evidence.title: JetStream: The Atmosphere
evidence.supports: Dry air is about 78.084% nitrogen, 20.946% oxygen, 0.934% argon and 0.042% carbon dioxide; water vapor varies and can reach about 4% of the volume; the atmosphere is rarely if ever dry.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 5 calls Biosphere 2 a closed system in which 'all the processes were contained within the model.' It was closed to matter but open to energy: sunlight entered through the glass and heat passed out. The oxygen story is also simplified: the carbon dioxide the soil microbes released was partly absorbed by exposed concrete, and managers eventually pumped in oxygen. The facility figures (3.14 acres, 3,800 species) and 'today it is a research facility' describe the time the textbook was written; the University of Arizona has run it since 2011.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content defines a closed system as closed to matter but open to energy. L10-Q26 asks what could still cross the sealed walls (sunlight and heat). L10-Q27 keys soil bacteria using oxygen (textbook-supported); L10-Q28 asks for the best hypothesis about the missing carbon dioxide and cites the external source. Acreage and species counts are not tested.

evidence.supports: Biosphere 2 was a physical model of Earth's biosphere; researchers monitored it for two years; after about sixteen months oxygen had declined, and the cause was traced to bacteria using oxygen to decompose organic matter.

evidence.title: Benchmarks: September 26, 1991: Crew sealed inside Biosphere 2
evidence.supports: Biosphere 2 was materially closed and energetically open, so only light and heat passed through its walls; oxygen fell from about 21% to about 14%; rich compost and peat soil drove high soil respiration; the gas reacted with exposed concrete; managers pumped in oxygen; the University of Arizona took over in 2011.

evidence.title: Biosphere 2: The Once Infamous Live-In Terrarium Is Transforming Climate Research
evidence.supports: The soil's thriving bacteria used up too much oxygen and the missing carbon dioxide had bonded with the building's concrete; today the University of Arizona runs Biosphere 2 as a climate research facility.

reviewFlags.issue: The Key Science Concept spread gives the biosphere as 'more than 70 km thick' and the hydrosphere as up to 20 km thick (5 km below the surface to 15 km up). These are rough model values with fuzzy edges; National Geographic describes the biosphere as about 20 km from top to bottom, with almost all life in a much thinner zone. The atmosphere's 10,000 km is a fading outer limit, not a sharp top.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question tests the biosphere, hydrosphere or atmosphere thickness numbers. Content labels them as the textbook's rough model values and says the atmosphere thins out gradually. Only the geosphere layer values (crust 35 km, mantle 2,865 km), which match standard figures closely, are used in a calculation (L10-Q05).

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept: The Flow of Energy and Matter Through Earth's Systems
evidence.supports: The spread labels the atmosphere about 10,000 km thick, the biosphere more than 70 km thick, the hydrosphere up to 20 km thick and the geosphere about 6,370 km thick.

evidence.title: Biosphere
evidence.supports: The biosphere measures about 20 km from top to bottom, and almost all life lives in a thinner zone from about 500 m below the ocean surface to about 6 km above sea level.

evidence.title: Mantle
evidence.supports: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick, consistent with the textbook's crust-plus-mantle depth.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 and its photo panel say about 97% of Earth's water is salty and 3% fresh, with fresh water split 69% glaciers, 30% groundwater and 1% lakes and rivers. USGS gives about 2.5% fresh water, and 68.7% / 30.1% / 1.2% for ice, groundwater and surface water: the same ranking, slightly different rounding.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says only a few percent of Earth's water is fresh. L10-Q06 asks only where most fresh water is found (glaciers and ice caps), a ranking both sources agree on; no question uses the exact percentages.

evidence.locator: Section 2. The Hydrosphere, The Parts of the Hydrosphere and photo panel
evidence.supports: Most of Earth's water is salt water; the small share that is fresh is mostly glacial ice, then groundwater, with very little in lakes and rivers.

evidence.title: Where is Earth's Water?
evidence.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School
evidence.supports: About 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh; of that, 68.7% is in ice caps and glaciers, 30.1% is groundwater and about 1.2% is surface water and other fresh water.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 1 compares the mantle's flow to cake batter and describes energy leaving the core 'by conduction'. Mantle rock is solid and deforms plastically over millions of years, far slower than any batter; the analogy can suggest the mantle is liquid. Within the mantle, convection carries much of the heat, which the textbook does acknowledge in Figure 1B.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says the mantle is solid rock that creeps very slowly and that one convection loop takes millions of years. L10-Q04 repairs the 'liquid magma mantle' misconception, and L10-Q25 names the speed and state difference as the key limit of a pot-of-water convection model.

evidence.locator: Section 1. The Geosphere, The Layers of the Geosphere and Figure 1B
evidence.supports: Mantle rock is solid but hot enough to flow very slowly; heated mantle rock rises and cooler, denser rock sinks in a convection cell.

evidence.title: Mantle
evidence.supports: The mantle is mostly solid rock that can move plastically over the course of millions of years; it is heated from below and cooled from above, and heat moves through it by convection.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 states that warm water is less dense than cold water without conditions. For fresh water this holds above about 4 °C; between 0 °C and 4 °C fresh water becomes less dense as it cools. The brief's seed question ('a suitably heated water container') needs that condition stated.
reviewFlags.resolution: The seed question L10-Q10 states its conditions (liquid water starting well above freezing, heated from below), and the L10-O2 explorer watch-out names the 4 °C exception.

evidence.locator: Section 2. The Hydrosphere, Energy and the Cycling of Matter in the Hydrosphere
evidence.supports: Warm water is less dense than cold water, so warm equatorial water stays near the ocean surface.

evidence.title: Water Density
evidence.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School
evidence.supports: Liquid water is densest at about 4 °C (39.2 °F) and becomes steadily less dense as it warms above that temperature.

reviewFlags.resolution: Every page of the lesson (128-139) was rendered at 110 dpi and read from the image. Diagram facts used in content (Figure 1A layer thicknesses, Figure 1B labels, Figure 2 current labels, Figure 3 convection-cell labels, Figure 4 arrows, the Key Science Concept thickness labels and captions) were taken from the renders, not the OCR.

evidence.locator: Figure 1B and Key Science Concept spread (rendered)
evidence.supports: Figure 1B labels: cooler material becomes denser and gravity pulls it toward Earth's center; warmer material becomes less dense and rises; internal energy flows outward by conduction. The spread says convection in the atmosphere and hydrosphere is driven by solar energy and gravity, and in the geosphere by internal energy and gravity.
